How Raspberry Pi 5 Handles Sustained Workloads

By Sam Example, 14 October 2026

Small single-board computers are often judged by short benchmarks that finish before the chip has had time to warm up. We wanted to know what happens when a Raspberry Pi 5 runs the same job for a full day, so we left one compiling a large codebase in a loop for twenty-four hours and logged its temperature, clock speed and throughput every ten seconds.

The setup

The board sat in a plain plastic case on a desk at room temperature, with the official active cooler fitted and the stock power supply. Nothing was overclocked. The storage was an NVMe drive on the PCIe adapter, which removes the microSD card as a bottleneck and makes the processor the part under test rather than the disk.

We measured three things: the reported SoC temperature, the ARM clock as seen by the firmware, and how many compile iterations completed per hour. A fall in iterations per hour would tell us that throttling was costing real work, not just a number on a dashboard.

What we saw

With the active cooler the board settled at a steady temperature within about fifteen minutes and stayed there. The fan cycled between its low and medium speeds and the clock never dropped below its rated maximum. Throughput across the day varied by less than two percent from hour to hour, which is within the noise of the build itself.

Without the cooler the story changed. The temperature climbed until the firmware started reducing the clock, and throughput fell by roughly a fifth once the board had been running for an hour. It never crashed, and it recovered as soon as the load stopped, but anyone planning to run long jobs should treat the cooler as part of the computer, not an accessory.

Takeaways

For always-on duties such as a home server, a network appliance or a small scraper, the Raspberry Pi 5 is comfortable as long as it can shed its heat. Leave headroom in memory and processor limits for the services that matter most, and watch the temperature for the first week so that you know what normal looks like before something goes wrong.
